BACKGROUND: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO 2 Rec) is slow in advanced heart failure. We sought to establish easily derived VO 2 Rec measures and evaluate their cardiospecificity and prognostic relevance in patients with dyspnea on exertion. We further sought to determine VO 2 Rec modifiability proportional to changes in cardiac function with disease-specific treatment of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. METHODS: VO 2 Rec patterns were evaluated in relation to cardiac performance and the primary outcome of heart failure hospitalization or death in a referral cohort with dyspnea on exertion undergoing cardiopulmonary exercise testing with hemodynamic monitoring (MGH-ExS [Massachusetts General Hospital Exercise Study]). We then investigated longitudinal measures of VO 2 Rec in the pivotal phase 3 randomized controlled trial SEQUOIA-HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) of aficamten versus placebo for 24 weeks in participants with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. For both cohorts, VO 2 Rec was uniformly measured as time for VO 2 to decline by >0%, 12.5% (VO 2 T 12.5% ), 25%, and 50% of peak VO 2 . RESULTS: Among 814 MGH-ExS patients (58±16 years of age, 58% women), those with a longer VO 2 T 12.5% (≥35 versus <35 seconds) demonstrated elevated exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure to cardiac output slope ( P <0.0001) with no difference in peripheral oxygen extraction ( P =0.11). For each 15-second increase in VO 2 T 12.5% , the hazard ratio for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death was 1.54 (95% CI, 1.35–1.76; P <0.001). In SEQUOIA-HCM participants with cardiopulmonary exercise testing at baseline and week 24 (n=263, 59.1±2.9 years of age, 41% women), baseline VO 2 T 12.5% was 45±20 seconds and improved 8 seconds (95% CI, −12 to −5 seconds; P <0.001) with aficamten treatment compared with placebo at 24 weeks. Participants treated with aficamten versus placebo were more likely to improve VO 2 T 12.5% by ≥15 seconds (odds ratio [OR], 3.7 [95% CI, 1.9–6.9]; number needed to treat=4.8). Shortening of VO 2 T 12.5% correlated with reduced NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I, and left ventricular outflow tract gradient (all P <005). CONCLUSIONS: This study established VO 2 T 12.5% as a new measure that reflects cardiac performance during exercise and predicted heart failure event-free survival. Furthermore, VO 2 T 12.5% improved proportional to improvements in left ventricular outflow tract gradient and cardiac biomarkers in response to aficamten treatment, a cardiospecific therapy for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The simplicity and physiological relevance of VO 2 T 12.5% support its regular inclusion in cardiopulmonary exercise testing protocols evaluating cardiac function during exercise. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05186818. aficamten cardiac myosin cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic exercise test heart failure, diastolic post-exercise recovery OPEN-ACCESS TRUE SDC T Clinical Perspective What Is New? This study reports multiple novel measures of oxygen uptake (VO 2 ) recovery after incremental exercise, highlighting that early VO2 recovery, measured as the time to recover 12.5% of peak VO2 (VO2T12.5%), is an easily derived measurement of metabolic resilience that closely reflects cardiac but not peripheral performance during exercise and predicts heart failure outcomes. In a separate clinical trial cohort from the SEQUOIA--HCM (Safety, Efficacy, and Quantitative Understanding of Obstruction Impact of Aficamten in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy) trial, we demonstrated that VO2T12.5% improves proportionate to improvements in cardiac function in response to aficamten treatment, a myocardial disease–specific intervention in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. What Are the Clinical Implications? Measurements of VO 2 recovery are not currently reported in cardiopulmonary exercise tests conducted in clinical practice or in clinical trials. VO 2 recovery assessment is noninvasive, simple to perform, and holds promise in helping to ascertain cardiospecific limitations to exercise capacity. VO2T12.5% complements other physiological measurements assessed during exercise and merits incorporation into cardiopulmonary exercise testing–based assessments of cardiac performance. VO2T12.5% deserves consideration as an important clinical trial end point when evaluating future cardiac interventions.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO2Rec) measures, especially VO2T12.5% (time to recover 12.5% of peak VO2), in patients with dyspnea on exertion (DOE) and obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). The research established VO2T12.5% as an easily derived, reliable, non-invasive biomarker that reflects cardiac performance, predicts heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death, and tracks with invasive hemodynamic indices. It differentiates impaired cardiac function in HFpEF and is modifiable by aficamten treatment in oHCM patients, improving proportionally to cardiac function and a reduction in cardiac biomarkers, indicating its utility as a prognostic and treatment response indicator. The study suggests its regular inclusion in cardiopulmonary exercise testing protocols.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Pharmacological treatment (Aficamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Aficamten was administered for 24 weeks in a phase 3 randomized controlled trial, compared against placebo. Doses were individualized to achieve the lowest effective dose, targeting a Valsalva Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Gradient (LVOT-G) <30 mm Hg while maintaining a left ventricular ejection fraction ">=\u00ad50%. Specific daily dosages (mg) and dose-response comparisons were not detailed, but treatment led to proportional improvements in cardiac function and biomarkers.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Longer/delayed (worse), improved/shorter (better) with treatment; prolonged duration (">=35 seconds) indicates worse cardiac function/outcomes; a reduced duration indicates improvement
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In MGH-ExS patients, a longer VO2T12.5% (">=35 seconds) was associated with elevated exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure to cardiac output slope (P <0.0001). For each 15-second increase in VO2T12.5%, the hazard ratio for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death was 1.54 (95% CI, 1.35	1.76; P <0.001). In SEQUOIA-HCM, baseline was 45	20 seconds and improved 8 seconds (95% CI, 	12 to 	5 seconds; P <0.001) with aficamten vs. placebo at 24 weeks. Aficamten-treated participants were 3.7 times more likely to improve VO2T12.5% by ">=15 seconds (OR, 3.7 [95% CI, 1.9	6.9]; NNT=4.8). Initial mean	SD 29	17 seconds in MGH-ExS cohort. Prolonged (">=35 seconds) associated with HR 2.52 [1.76	3.62] for adverse outcomes, modestly attenuated to 1.76 [1.20	2.60] (P=0.003) after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI. An average relative magnitude of 18% improvement was observed in response to aficamten treatment. VO2T12.5% ">=35 seconds predicted all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization. analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery, an indicator of metabolic resilience and cardiac performance. Captures metabolic consequences of increasing metabolic rate during exercise, provides a quantitative measure of metabolic resilience, and reflects cardiocentric exercise limitations. Indicator of early oxygen uptake recovery kinetics, reflecting the efficiency of the cardiovascular system to restore baseline metabolic state after exercise. Integrates cardiovascular and metabolic responses.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery during cardiopulmonary exercise testing; response to aficamten treatment for obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). Post-exercise recovery in patients with dyspnea on exertion (DOE), established severe heart failure (HF), and symptomatic oHCM. Early recovery from incremental ramp exercise; aficamten treatment in oHCM patients; differentiation of HFpEF-HDI from NCD. Dyspneic individuals with HFpEF; symptomatic oHCM; cardiac myosin inhibition treatment (aficamten); evaluation of cardiac reserve capacity during exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects cardiac performance during exercise, predicts heart failure event-free survival, indicates cardiospecific limitations to exercise capacity, and is a potential endpoint for cardiac interventions. Prolonged VO2Rec is linked to worse cardiac output augmentation during exercise and increased risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes (HF hospitalization and all-cause death), independent of peak VO2. It serves as a sensitive noninvasive surrogate for identifying impaired cardiac performance during exercise. Discriminates impaired central cardiac function in HFpEF-HDI (AUC 0.72 vs 0.63 for VO2 T 0%, P <0.001). Prolonged VO2 T 12.5% (">=35 seconds) predicts increased risk for heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death. Improvement with aficamten treatment is associated with reduced NT-proBNP, hs-cTnI, and LVOT-G. Identifies impaired cardiac performance in HFpEF, predicts all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization, risk-stratifies individuals with impaired peak VO2 or elevated NT-proBNP with underlying symptomatic HFpEF, indicates responsiveness to cardiac-specific treatment, and prolonged VO2T12.5% relates to elevated filling pressures. Should be considered for inclusion in standard CPET protocols; promising noninvasive measurement for defining impaired cardiac performance in human cardiac drug development randomized controlled trials.
